title: WHEN GOD SAID, “PUT THE BLOOD ON THE DOOR.”
paragraphs: WHEN GOD SAID, “PUT THE BLOOD ON THE DOOR.”
One night in Egypt, the difference between life and death was not wealth.

It was not strength.
It was not power.
It was not even morality.
The difference was blood on a doorpost.
God gave Israel a strange instruction before the final plague came upon Egypt.
Every household was commanded to take a spotless lamb, sacrifice it, and place its blood on the two doorposts and the top beam of the house.
Then God made a promise that would echo through history:
“When I see the blood, I will pass over you.” — Exodus 12:13
That night, judgment swept through Egypt.
But something remarkable happened.

Where the blood was present…
death did not enter.
The destroyer did not examine the house.
He did not check the morality of the family inside.
He did not inspect their past.
He looked for one thing only.
The blood.
But here is something many people miss about that night.
The Israelites were not saved because they were better than the Egyptians.
They were saved because a lamb had died in their place.
Inside every protected home, a lamb had already paid the price.
That is the heart of Passover.
Substitution.
A life given so another life could be spared.
The firstborn inside the house lived because the lamb had died outside.
And God established this event as a memorial for generations.
Every year, Israel would remember that night.
Every year they would remember the lamb.
Every year they would remember the blood.
But Passover was never just about Egypt.
It was a prophecy.
Centuries later, another Lamb would appear.
When John the Baptist saw Jesus, he made a powerful declaration:
“Behold, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.” — John 1:29
John was pointing back to Passover.

Jesus was not just a teacher.
Not just a prophet.
He was the Lamb.
The true sacrifice that Passover had been pointing toward for centuries.
Just as the Passover lamb had to be without defect (Exodus 12:5), Jesus lived a sinless life.
Just as the lamb’s blood protected households from judgment, Christ’s blood protects believers from the judgment of sin.
And just as the Israelites had to apply the blood to their door, salvation requires more than simply knowing the story.
It requires trusting in the sacrifice God provided.
Think about the tension in those homes on that night.
Parents sitting inside.
Children waiting.
Outside, Egypt was about to experience the most devastating night in its history.
But inside the houses marked by blood, there was protection.
Not because the door was strong.
Not because the family was perfect.
But because the blood had already answered the judgment.
Here is a powerful truth many people overlook.
God did not say:
“When I see your effort.”
He did not say:
“When I see your goodness.”
He said:
“When I see the blood.”
That was the sign.
That was the covering.
That was the difference.
Passover reveals something about the heart of God.
God is both just and merciful.
Justice requires that sin has consequences.
But mercy provides a substitute.
At Passover, the substitute was a lamb.
At the cross, the substitute was Christ Himself.
That is why the apostle Paul later wrote:
“Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.” — 1 Corinthians 5:7
The story that began in Exodus finds its fulfillment at the cross.
The blood on the doorposts pointed forward to the blood on the cross.
One protected from physical death.
The other offers rescue from eternal separation from God.
Another detail is easy to miss.
God did not tell the Israelites to admire the lamb.
He told them to apply the blood.
The protection was not theoretical.
It had to be personally applied to the house.
In the same way, the message of the cross is not just information.
It is an invitation.
An invitation to trust in the sacrifice God provided.
That night in Egypt, there were only two types of houses.
Houses with blood on the door.
And houses without it.
The difference between the two was everything.
And the lesson still echoes today.
Not every door in Egypt was marked.
But every door could have been.
The invitation of salvation has always been open.
The question has never been whether the sacrifice was sufficient.
The question is whether the blood has been applied.
The Passover story reminds us of something powerful:
Deliverance did not come from human strength.
It came from God’s provision.
The lamb.
The blood.
The promise.
And on that dark night in Egypt, one sentence carried the hope of an entire nation:
“When I see the blood, I will pass over you.”
What is the most powerful lesson you see in the story of Passover?
